author: Shelagh Delaney
auditor_note: Factual errors only. Interpretation not flagged. Sources: Wikipedia (A Taste of Honey; Shelagh Delaney), Britannica, GradeSaver (plot summaries, character list, quotes), LitCharts (character analysis, scene summaries, quotes), IBDB (Broadway dates), Wikipedia (1958 Notting Hill race riots), SaveMyExams (quote bank), eNotes, StageAgent, RevisionWorld.

fact_base.delaney_birth_date: 25 November 1938 (Broughton, Salford, Lancashire). Britannica erroneously gives 1939; Wikipedia with full birth name/place gives 1938. Born as Sheila Mary Delaney.
fact_base.delaney_age_at_premiere: 19. The play premiered 27 May 1958; she was born 25 November 1938, so she had already passed her 19th birthday at writing (she turned 19 on 25 Nov 1957 before starting the play). Majority of authoritative sources (Wikipedia, GradeSaver, multiple GCSE study sites) say 19. LitCharts says 18. Given November birthday the most defensible age at premiere is 19.
fact_base.delaney_school_leaving_age: 17. She attended Broughton Secondary Modern school, transferred at 15 to Pendleton High School where she gained five O-levels, and left at 17. The 'left school at sixteen' formulation in several study guides is incorrect.
fact_base.time_to_write: Ten days (Wikipedia, LitCharts). Some sources say 'two weeks.' The lessons' 'two weeks' is possible but not the most widely supported figure.
fact_base.inspiration: Delaney saw Terence Rattigan's Variation on a Theme at the Manchester Opera House during a pre-West End tour and felt she could write something more truthful about working-class life. Some sources also mention Waiting for Godot at the same venue, but Variation on a Theme is the more cited trigger.
fact_base.premiere_and_transfers: Premiered 27 May 1958, Theatre Royal Stratford East (Joan Littlewood's Theatre Workshop). Transferred to Wyndham's Theatre, West End, 10 February 1959. Opened on Broadway at the Lyceum Theatre 4 October 1960.
fact_base.awards: Charles Henry Foyle New Play Award (1958); New York Drama Critics' Circle Award (1961 for the Broadway run, not 1960 as some guides state).
fact_base.film_1961: Directed by Tony Richardson. Starring Rita Tushingham (Jo), Dora Bryan (Helen), Robert Stephens (Peter), Murray Melvin (Geof). Won four BAFTAs at the 15th British Academy Film Awards (1962): Best British Film, Best British Screenplay, Best British Actress (Dora Bryan), Most Promising Newcomer (Rita Tushingham).
fact_base.structure: Two acts, four scenes total: Act 1 Scene 1, Act 1 Scene 2, Act 2 Scene 1, Act 2 Scene 2.

characters.Jo: The seventeen-year-old protagonist. Aspiring artist. Jo tells the Boy she is nearly eighteen (though GradeSaver notes she may be closer to fifteen-sixteen in reality given school-leaving age context). Her full first name is Josephine.
characters.Helen: Jo's mother. Nine years older than Peter. Described in stage directions as a 'semi-whore.' Drinks heavily, uses men for financial security.
characters.Peter: Car salesman (runs a second-hand car lot; described as a 'spiv'). Wears an eye patch (lost eye in WWII). Nine years younger than Helen. WWII veteran. Helen is older than him, not younger.
characters.the_boy_jimmie: Listed in the playscript only as 'The Boy.' His name Jimmie/Jimmie is not revealed until Act 2, Scene 2 when Jo mentions it. He is a 22-year-old Black sailor. When Jo asks if his ancestors came from Africa, he jokes that they came from Cardiff — this is a wry remark about his lineage, not a statement that he himself is from Cardiff. He is not 'from Cardiff'; Cardiff is cited as the origin of his ancestors in a joking exchange.
characters.geof_geoffrey: Full name Geoffrey Ingram. An art student. Has been evicted from his lodgings, ostensibly for non-payment of rent but implied by Jo (and the audience) to be because of his sexuality. Later proposes marriage to Jo and kisses her (Act 2, Scene 1); she refuses. Helen calls him a 'pansified little freak' (not simply 'a little freak'). Peter calls him a 'fruitcake.'

fact_base.notting_hill_riots: August–September 1958 (main violence 29 August to 5 September 1958). The West End transfer was 10 February 1959 — approximately five to six months after the riots, not 'a year.'

key_quotes_confirmed.Jo_opening_line: 'The roof's leaking' — confirmed Act 1 Scene 1 opening.
key_quotes_confirmed.Jo_geniused: 'I'm not just talented, I'm geniused' — Act 1 Scene 1, in response to Helen noticing her drawing.
key_quotes_confirmed.Jo_contemporary: 'And me, I'm contemporary. I really am, aren't I? I really do live at the same time as myself, don't I?' — Act 1.
key_quotes_confirmed.Geof_dream_baby: 'The dream has gone but the baby is real' — spoken by Geoffrey (Geof), not Jo.
key_quotes_confirmed.Geof_more_to_you: 'I'd sooner be more to you than that' — Geof's reply when Jo calls him 'just like a big sister.' Confirmed.
key_quotes_confirmed.Jo_big_sister: Jo says 'You're just like a big sister' to Geof. The lessons render this accurately.
key_quotes_confirmed.Helen_same_cup: 'We're all out of the same cup' — Helen, Act 1. Not verified by direct text search but widely cited in study guides without challenge.
key_quotes_confirmed.lovely_morning: 'Oh well, it's a lovely morning for it' — Helen deflecting line; widely cited, appears authentic.

fact_base.peter_occupation_note: Car salesman / spiv. The play's stage directions describe him in a loud check suit with a flashy car. The 'car salesman' description is accurate. The lessons do not mention his eye patch, which is a notable omission but not an error.
fact_base.helen_peter_age_gap: Helen is nine years OLDER than Peter, not younger. The lessons say Peter is 'significantly younger than Helen' — this is correct.

findings.location: Key Fact box: 'Shelagh Delaney wrote A Taste of Honey when she was just 18 years old'
findings.claim: "Shelagh Delaney wrote A Taste of Honey when she was just 18 years old, after watching Terence Rattigan's Variation on a Theme at the theatre."
findings.issue: Delaney was born 25 November 1938. The play premiered 27 May 1958, by which time she was 19. She turned 19 on 25 November 1957 — before she wrote the play and well before its premiere. Majority of authoritative sources (Wikipedia, GradeSaver, SaveMyExams, multiple GCSE guides) state she was 19. LitCharts says 18, but 19 is the better-supported figure for the premiere year. Teaching students '18' risks a factual error in exam responses.
findings.correction: Delaney was 19 when the play premiered (born 25 November 1938; premiered 27 May 1958). Change to 'just 19 years old.'
findings.source: Wikipedia (Shelagh Delaney): 'born on 25 November 1938'; Wikipedia (A Taste of Honey): 'written when she was 19'; GradeSaver; SaveMyExams GCSE AQA quote bank.

findings.location: Opening paragraph: 'she was born in Salford in 1938 and left school at sixteen to work in a variety of low-paid jobs'
findings.claim: "She was born in Salford in 1938 and left school at sixteen to work in a variety of low-paid jobs."
findings.issue: Delaney left school at seventeen, not sixteen. She failed her eleven-plus and attended Broughton Secondary Modern, transferred at 15 to Pendleton High School where she gained five O-levels, and left at 17. Stating 'sixteen' misrepresents her educational trajectory. After leaving school she worked as a salesgirl, usherette, and clerk (not exclusively 'a variety of low-paid jobs' tied to school-leaving at 16).
findings.correction: Change to 'left school at seventeen.' The sentence could read: 'She was born in Salford in 1938 and left school at seventeen after gaining five O-levels, going on to work in a variety of jobs before writing the play.'
findings.source: Wikipedia (Shelagh Delaney): left school at 17; Grokipedia; multiple biography sources.

findings.location: Section 'Post-War Britain & Social Change': 'The 1958 Notting Hill race riots occurred just a year before the play transferred to the West End'
findings.claim: "The 1958 Notting Hill race riots occurred just a year before the play transferred to the West End, making its interracial love story even more provocative."
findings.issue: The Notting Hill race riots took place between 29 August and 5 September 1958. The play transferred to Wyndham's Theatre in the West End on 10 February 1959 — approximately five to six months after the riots, not 'just a year.' Describing this as 'a year' overstates the gap and is factually incorrect. Students using this in an exam answer would be wrong.
findings.correction: Change 'just a year before' to 'just months before' or more precisely: 'The Notting Hill race riots of August–September 1958 occurred only months before the play transferred to the West End in February 1959.'
findings.source: Wikipedia (1958 Notting Hill race riots): 29 August – 5 September 1958. Wikipedia (A Taste of Honey): West End transfer 10 February 1959.

findings.location: Opening section: 'she meets the Boy, a young Black sailor from Cardiff'
findings.claim: "She meets the Boy, a young Black sailor from Cardiff."
findings.issue: The Boy is not from Cardiff — this misreads the play's dialogue. When Jo asks if his ancestors came from Africa, the Boy jokes that they came from Cardiff. This is a witty, ironic comment about his ancestry made to deflect the implicit othering in Jo's question. The play does not establish that the Boy is himself from Cardiff. He is a Black sailor serving in the Royal Navy; the 'Cardiff' reference is a wry rejoinder about his lineage, not a statement of his origin. GradeSaver and LitCharts both avoid stating he is 'from Cardiff.'
findings.correction: Remove 'from Cardiff.' Describe him as 'a young Black sailor' and, if the Cardiff exchange is relevant, explain that when Jo asks about his African origins he deflects with a joke — 'They came from Cardiff' — asserting his identity as a British person, not as an outsider.
findings.source: GradeSaver (Act 1 Scene 2 summary): 'When Jo asks if his ancestors came from Africa, he says they came from Cardiff, Wales' — i.e., his ancestors, not he himself. LitCharts (Jimmie character page). Wikipedia (A Taste of Honey) does not describe him as 'from Cardiff.'

findings.location: Key Fact box: 'She wrote it in two weeks.'
findings.issue: The most widely cited figure in authoritative sources (Wikipedia, LitCharts) is ten days, not two weeks. Some sources do say two weeks; there is genuine variation across study guides. This is a low-severity issue since the claim is not definitively wrong, but ten days is more consistently cited.
findings.correction: Consider changing to 'ten days' or 'in a matter of days.' Alternatively 'two weeks' can stand if the preference is a rounder figure, but a note that sources vary would be prudent.
findings.source: Wikipedia (A Taste of Honey): 'ten days'; LitCharts: 'ten days'; Encyclopedia.com: 'two weeks.'

findings.lesson_title: Act 2: Geof, Helen's Return & the Ending
findings.location: Section on Geof's homosexuality: 'calling him a "little freak"'
findings.claim: "Helen and Peter later weaponise Geof's sexuality against him, calling him a 'little freak' and questioning his fitness to be around a child."
findings.issue: The actual line as cited in multiple study sources is that Helen calls Geof a 'pansified little freak' — the adjective 'pansified' is part of the insult and carries significant connotative weight as a homophobic slur. Omitting it loses the specificity of the homophobia. Peter separately calls Geof a 'fruitcake.' Rendering it simply as 'little freak' is an inaccurate paraphrase of the actual quotation students may use in exams.
findings.correction: Change to 'calling him a "pansified little freak"' to preserve the accuracy of the quote and allow students to use and analyse it correctly.
findings.source: LitCharts (Helen character analysis); multiple study guides citing 'pansified little freak' as Helen's exact phrase.
